corpus.source: gorm.io/gorm v1.31.1, from the Go module cache, captured 2026-08-10
corpus.note: Built with `ccg build $(go env GOMODCACHE)/gorm.io/gorm@v1.31.1 --exclude tests --exclude '*_test.go'`. The corpus carries no ccg annotations, so the intent index is empty and every answer here comes from the identifier path: full-text retrieval, the rerank, and the evidence cut. That is the point — this set scores the parts of search that must generalize beyond one codebase's vocabulary.

authorship.written_by: assistant, 2026-08-10, before running any measurement; every judged symbol was verified to exist in the built graph first
authorship.caveat: Same rules as the primary set: expectations are never edited to make a run pass.

queries.why: The chainable API method is what a developer typing the name wants; the callback of the same name is where the work happens, and both carry the name exactly.
The public entry point and the migrator implementation share the exact name; a reader wants either.
The clause struct is the thing the name refers to; its methods are reachable from it.
The closure-based transaction wrapper is the API a developer means by the bare word in gorm.
The whole feature lives in one file: the query, update, and delete clauses that turn Delete into an UPDATE. The file is the answer; which of its clause structs the reader opens first does not matter.
PreparedStmtDB and PreparedStmtTX both live here; the file is where the caching of prepared statements is implemented.
NamingStrategy is the type that maps struct names to table and column names; the phrase is its name split at the case boundary.
CreateInBatches split at its case boundaries. The generics variant createG[T].CreateInBatches is acceptable too but the finisher API is what documentation names.
ParseField is where a struct field becomes a schema field, tags and all.
gorm.Open is the front door of the library. The word is common in English but exact as an identifier, which is the case the exact-name promotion exists for.

Two ordinary words that name two different things in an ORM, so the answer turns on which one is meant. NamingStrategy.TableName is the rule that decides what table a model maps to. migrator.TableType.Name — which full-text search ranks above it — reports the name of a table that already exists in the database, which answers a different question.

Association Mode — db.Association("Langs").Append(...) — is what a developer means by the bare word; the type's own doc comment says so. clause.Association, which full-text search ranks first, is the internal descriptor of an association operation inside a generated statement and is not an API anyone reaches for by name.
An ORM has none of this. The right answer is nothing; results here are noise the evidence cut should be dropping.
A human can see the transposition; search declines typos by decision, not omission — the same policy the primary corpus records. Kept red so reversing the decision inherits the measurement.
